lessonTitle: Gram-Positive Pathogens: Staphylococci, Streptococci and Clostridia

blocks.text: A 22-year-old rugby player has a hot, tender swelling on his thigh that drains pus, and his swab grows golden colonies of Gram-positive cocci in tight clusters. Elsewhere on the same ward, another patient with a deep contaminated wound develops a rigid jaw. Both infections are caused by Gram-positive bacteria, yet one is mainly invasive and the other almost entirely toxin-driven. What the organism makes can matter more than the organism.

blocks.markdown: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall and no outer membrane, so they have no endotoxin; their virulence relies on **surface proteins, capsules and exotoxins**. We cover three groups: **staphylococci** (cocci in clusters, catalase-positive), **streptococci** (cocci in chains or pairs, catalase-negative) and **clostridia** (anaerobic spore-forming bacilli).

blocks.title: Coagulase
blocks.text: Coagulase is an enzyme that converts fibrinogen to fibrin, clotting plasma. The coagulase test divides staphylococci: Staphylococcus aureus is coagulase-positive; coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS), such as S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus, are coagulase-negative.

blocks.caption: Staphylococci compared
rows: Often golden, beta-haemolytic on blood agar
Protein A, toxins (TSST-1, enterotoxins, exfoliative toxins), invasive enzymes
Fewer toxins; adhere to plastic and form biofilm (S. epidermidis)
Skin abscess, impetigo, wound infection, endocarditis, osteomyelitis, toxin syndromes
S. epidermidis: infections of catheters and prosthetic devices; S. saprophyticus: cystitis in young women
True pathogen when isolated from blood
Skin commensals; frequent blood culture contaminants

blocks.markdown: *S. aureus* causes disease in two ways: **direct invasion** (abscess, wound infection, bacteraemia with seeding to bone, joints and heart valves) and **toxins**. Pre-formed heat-stable **enterotoxins** cause food poisoning with onset 1-6 hours after eating and no fever. **Toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1)** is a superantigen that cross-links the T-cell receptor and MHC class II outside the usual peptide groove, activating large numbers of T cells and causing massive cytokine release, fever, rash and shock. **Exfoliative toxins** cleave desmoglein in the epidermis, causing staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome. CoNS are important mainly in patients with prosthetic material, where **biofilm** protects them.

blocks.title: Interpreting a blood culture
blocks.prompt: One of four blood culture bottles from a well patient grows Gram-positive cocci in clusters that are coagulase-negative. A second patient with a prosthetic heart valve has all four bottles grow clustered Gram-positive cocci that are coagulase-positive. Interpret each.

steps.text: Clusters point to Staphylococcus. Coagulase separates S. aureus (positive) from CoNS (negative).
A single bottle of a CoNS in a well patient is most likely skin contamination, since CoNS are skin commensals.
Coagulase-positive staphylococci in all bottles is S. aureus bacteraemia, always significant, with a risk of endocarditis in a patient with a valve.

blocks.answer: Patient 1: probable contaminant. Patient 2: true S. aureus bacteraemia needing urgent assessment.

blocks.markdown: **Streptococci** are classified in two complementary ways. **Haemolysis on blood agar**: *alpha* (partial, green discolouration), *beta* (complete clearing) and *gamma* (none). **Lancefield grouping** uses antibodies against the cell wall carbohydrate antigen and applies chiefly to beta-haemolytic streptococci. Group A (*Streptococcus pyogenes*, bacitracin-sensitive) causes pharyngitis, impetigo, cellulitis, necrotising fasciitis and scarlet fever, and immune-mediated sequelae (rheumatic fever and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis). Group B (*S. agalactiae*) colonises the vagina and causes neonatal sepsis and meningitis. Alpha-haemolytic *Streptococcus pneumoniae* (optochin-sensitive, encapsulated, not Lancefield grouped) causes pneumonia, meningitis and otitis media; viridans streptococci are mouth flora that can cause endocarditis.

blocks.caption: Streptococcal classification
rows: Urinary tract and biliary infection, endocarditis

blocks.markdown: **Clostridia** are Gram-positive, obligately anaerobic, spore-forming bacilli. Spores survive in soil and heat. Their diseases are **toxin-mediated**. *C. tetani* grows in a contaminated wound and releases **tetanospasmin**, which travels in retrograde fashion to the central nervous system and blocks release of the inhibitory neurotransmitters glycine and GABA at spinal interneurons, leading to **spastic paralysis** (trismus, risus sardonicus, opisthotonos). *C. botulinum* produces **botulinum toxin**, which blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, causing **flaccid paralysis**; it is acquired from improperly preserved food or in infants. *C. perfringens* produces **alpha toxin (a lecithinase)** and causes gas gangrene (myonecrosis) in dead tissue, and a food-poisoning enterotoxin. *C. difficile* causes antibiotic-associated colitis through toxins A and B.

blocks.caption: Toxin-mediated clostridial diseases
rows: Toxins A and B damage colonic epithelium

blocks.title: Rapid growth in anaerobic tissue
blocks.prompt: A deep wound contains 50 vegetative C. perfringens cells. In necrotic anaerobic tissue the organism has a generation time of 10 minutes. How many cells after 2 hours, assuming exponential growth?
blocks.answer: About 2.0 x 10^5 cells, showing how fast gas gangrene can progress.

items: Coagulase-positive cocci in clusters: S. aureus. Coagulase-negative: CoNS.
Beta-haemolytic group A: S. pyogenes; group B: S. agalactiae.
Alpha-haemolytic: S. pneumoniae (optochin-sensitive) and viridans streptococci.
Tetanus: spastic paralysis; botulism: flaccid paralysis.
Gas gangrene: C. perfringens alpha toxin.

blocks.title: Toxins explain the syndromes
blocks.text: Tetanospasmin and botulinum toxin act on the same type of process (neurotransmitter release) but at opposite synapses, which is why one causes spasm and the other paralysis.

blocks.title: Pitfalls
blocks.text: A coagulase-negative staphylococcus in one blood culture bottle is often a contaminant, but not always in a patient with a prosthesis. Alpha-haemolysis is not a Lancefield group, and S. pneumoniae is not group-typed by Lancefield antigen.

points: S. aureus is coagulase-positive and toxin-producing; CoNS are skin commensals that cause device infection.
Streptococci are classified by haemolysis (alpha, beta, gamma) and by Lancefield carbohydrate group.
Clostridia are anaerobic spore formers whose diseases are toxin-mediated: tetanus (spastic), botulism (flaccid), gas gangrene, C. difficile colitis.

questions.stem: Which test best separates Staphylococcus aureus from coagulase-negative staphylococci?

options.text: Coagulase test
Oxidase test
Optochin sensitivity
Lancefield grouping

distractorRationale.b: Oxidase distinguishes groups such as Neisseria and Pseudomonas.

questions.explanation: S. aureus produces coagulase, which clots plasma, whereas CoNS do not. This is the standard way to separate the two groups.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a recently inserted central venous catheter has fever. Blood cultures from the line and a peripheral vein both grow coagulase-negative cocci in clusters. Which organism and explanation fit best?

options.text: Staphylococcus epidermidis, a skin commensal that forms biofilm on plastic devices
Staphylococcus aureus, because it is coagulase-negative
Streptococcus pyogenes, because it forms clusters
Clostridium perfringens, because it is Gram-positive

questions.correctOptionText: Staphylococcus epidermidis, a skin commensal that forms biofilm on plastic devices
questions.explanation: CoNS such as S. epidermidis colonise skin and attach to catheters. Growth from multiple sets suggests true infection rather than contamination.

questions.stem: A throat swab grows beta-haemolytic cocci in chains that are bacitracin-sensitive. Which Lancefield group and organism does this indicate?

options.text: Group A, Streptococcus pyogenes
Group B, Streptococcus agalactiae
Alpha-haemolytic Streptococcus pneumoniae
Staphylococcus aureus

distractorRationale.b: Group B streptococci are bacitracin-resistant and colonise the genital tract.
distractorRationale.c: S. pneumoniae is alpha-haemolytic and optochin-sensitive.
distractorRationale.d: S. aureus forms clusters and is coagulase-positive.

questions.explanation: Beta-haemolysis with chains and bacitracin sensitivity identifies group A streptococcus. Lancefield grouping is based on the cell wall carbohydrate antigen.

questions.stem: Which statement about Streptococcus pneumoniae is correct?

options.text: It is alpha-haemolytic, optochin-sensitive and not assigned a Lancefield group
It is beta-haemolytic and belongs to Lancefield group A
It is gamma-haemolytic and belongs to group D
It is a coagulase-positive coccus in clusters

questions.correctOptionText: It is alpha-haemolytic, optochin-sensitive and not assigned a Lancefield group

distractorRationale.c: Group D enterococci are typically non-haemolytic.

questions.explanation: Pneumococci cause partial (alpha) haemolysis and are encapsulated. They are identified by optochin sensitivity and bile solubility rather than Lancefield typing.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old unvaccinated farmer lacerates his forearm on a plough. Ten days later he has a stiff jaw, painful muscle spasms and an arched back, with a clear sensorium. Which toxin action explains his illness?

options.text: Tetanospasmin blocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitters (glycine and GABA)
Botulinum toxin blocks release of acetylcholine
Alpha toxin destroys cell membranes in muscle
Toxin A damages colonic epithelium

questions.correctOptionText: Tetanospasmin blocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitters (glycine and GABA)

distractorRationale.a: Correct: loss of inhibition causes spastic paralysis.
distractorRationale.b: Botulinum toxin causes flaccid, not spastic, paralysis.
distractorRationale.c: Alpha toxin causes gas gangrene, with local tissue destruction.
distractorRationale.d: Toxin A is the C. difficile enterotoxin.

questions.explanation: Clostridium tetani grows in the anaerobic wound and releases tetanospasmin, which ascends to the central nervous system. Blocking inhibitory interneuron transmitters produces unopposed muscle contraction.

questions.stem: After a banquet, 24 of 60 guests who ate the chicken salad developed vomiting within 4 hours, compared with 3 of 40 guests who did not eat it. Calculate the relative risk of illness for those who ate the chicken salad (risk in exposed divided by risk in unexposed).
questions.explanation: Risk in exposed = 24/60 = 0.40; risk in unexposed = 3/40 = 0.075. Relative risk = 0.40 / 0.075 = 5.33, which implicates the chicken salad; the rapid onset fits pre-formed Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin.

questions.stem: A necrotic wound contains 20 vegetative Clostridium perfringens cells. In anaerobic tissue the generation time is 15 minutes. Assuming exponential growth and no lag, how many cells are present after 3 hours?
questions.explanation: Three hours is 180 minutes, giving 180/15 = 12 generations. N = 20 x 2^12 = 20 x 4096 = 81 920 cells, which illustrates the speed of toxin-producing growth in dead tissue.

questions.stem: Describe how Staphylococcus aureus differs from coagulase-negative staphylococci in virulence and clinical significance when isolated from blood.
markingGuide: S. aureus is coagulase-positive; CoNS are coagulase-negative
S. aureus has many virulence factors: protein A, toxins (TSST-1, enterotoxins, exfoliative toxin) and invasive disease
CoNS are skin commensals with limited virulence
CoNS cause device-related infection through biofilm (S. epidermidis); S. saprophyticus causes cystitis
S. aureus in blood is never ignored; single-bottle CoNS is often a contaminant
questions.explanation: The key distinction is clinical: S. aureus is a true pathogen whereas CoNS usually are not unless prosthetic material is present. The coagulase test is the laboratory marker.

questions.stem: Explain how streptococci are classified by haemolysis and by Lancefield grouping, giving one example of each category and one disease.
markingGuide: Alpha: partial haemolysis (green), such as S. pneumoniae, causing pneumonia
Beta: complete haemolysis, such as S. pyogenes (group A) causing pharyngitis, or S. agalactiae (group B) causing neonatal sepsis
Gamma: no haemolysis, such as Enterococcus
Lancefield grouping is based on cell wall carbohydrate antigen detected by antibodies
Lancefield grouping mainly applies to beta-haemolytic streptococci; S. pneumoniae is not grouped
questions.explanation: Haemolysis is observed on blood agar; Lancefield group is an immunological property. Combining them gives a practical identification scheme.

questions.stem: Contrast the toxin-mediated diseases tetanus and botulism, explaining why one causes spastic and the other flaccid paralysis, and name one other toxin-mediated clostridial disease.
markingGuide: Tetanus: C. tetani in a wound; tetanospasmin travels to the central nervous system
Tetanospasmin blocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitters (glycine, GABA), giving unopposed contraction and spastic paralysis
Botulism: C. botulinum toxin from food or infant gut
Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, giving flaccid paralysis
Another example: C. perfringens alpha toxin (gas gangrene) or C. difficile toxins A and B (colitis)
questions.explanation: Both toxins block neurotransmitter release but at different synapses: inhibitory in the spinal cord for tetanus, excitatory at the neuromuscular junction for botulism. This explains the opposite clinical pictures.
